pg_21__page_28_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two density curves labeled (a) Wage density and (b) Log wage density, showing the distribution of wages and log wages.

Plot (a) Wage density shows a strongly right-skewed distribution on a horizontal axis ranging from 0 to 70. The peak of the density occurs near 15, after which the curve steadily decreases with a long right tail extending toward 70.

Plot (b) Log wage density shows a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution on a horizontal axis ranging from 0 to 6. The distribution is centered with its peak around 3, with small tails on either side and a tiny secondary bump near 5.

pg_21__page_29_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two density plots labeled (a) Women and men, and (b) By gender and race, illustrating log wage distributions.

Plot (a) shows two bell-shaped probability density curves representing log wages for 'Women' and 'Men'. The x-axis ranges from 0 to 6 with tick marks at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Both distributions peak near a value of 3. The curve for women is shifted slightly to the left and has a slightly higher peak than the curve for men, indicating slightly lower average log wages for women.

Plot (b) breaks down the distribution into four overlapping curves labeled 'Black women', 'White women', 'Black men', and 'White men'. The x-axis ranges from 1 to 5 with ticks at 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. From left to right along the left slope, the curves peak and transition sequentially: Black women are furthest to the left, followed closely by White women, then Black men, and finally White men furthest to the right, showing that White men have the highest relative log wage distribution.

pg_21__page_33_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A line plot titled 'FIGURE 2.3 Expected log wage as a function of education'. The vertical axis (y-axis) represents 'Log dollars per hour' ranging from 2.0 to 4.0 in increments of 0.5. The horizontal axis (x-axis) represents 'Education (years)' ranging from 4 to 20 years with tick marks at 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20.

The graph contains two upward-sloping series:
1. 'Men' (marked with solid circles): Starts near 2.38 log dollars at 4 years of education, remains flat through 6 years, rises to ~2.52 at 8 years, slightly dips to ~2.44 at 9 years, then steadily climbs to ~2.58 at 10–11 years, ~2.84 at 12 years, ~2.98 at 13 years, ~3.06 at 14 years, ~3.35 at 16 years, ~3.53 at 18 years, and reaches a peak of ~3.83 at 20 years.
2. 'Women' (marked with solid triangles): Follows a parallel path beneath Men, starting around 2.15 log dollars at 4 years, staying around 2.20 through 8 years, dipping to ~2.13 at 9 years, rising to ~2.30 at 10–11 years, then climbing steadily to ~2.58 at 12 years, ~2.71 at 13 years, ~2.84 at 14 years, ~3.05 at 16 years, ~3.23 at 18 years, and reaching ~3.52 at 20 years.

Overall, both curves demonstrate a strong positive relationship between years of education and log hourly earnings, with men's log wages consistently higher than women's log wages across all education levels.

pg_21__page_35_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two related plots depicting the relationship between log wage and labor market experience.

Graph (a) is titled "Joint density of log wage and experience". The x-axis represents "Labor market experience (years)" ranging from 0 to 45 in increments of 5. The y-axis represents "Log dollars per hour" ranging from 2.0 to 3.5 in increments of 0.5. It displays a set of contour lines representing a two-dimensional joint probability density function. A line passing through the contours indicates the "Conditional expectation" of log wage given experience, which rises initially from around 2.0 to near 3.0 at 25–30 years of experience, and then levels off / slightly decreases.

Graph (b) is titled "Conditional density of log wage given experience". The x-axis represents "Log dollars per hour" ranging from 1.0 to 4.5 in increments of 0.5. It shows three univariate bell-shaped density curves corresponding to fixed levels of experience X:
- Curve for X = 5: centered at a lower peak around 2.6 log dollars per hour, with a slightly taller maximum height.
- Curve for X = 10: shifted slightly to the right, centered around 2.7 log dollars per hour.
- Curve for X = 25: shifted furthest to the right, centered around 2.9 log dollars per hour, with a lower peak and slightly wider spread.

pg_21__page_38_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A 2D contour plot (density plot) titled 'FIGURE 2.5 Joint density of regression error and experience'. The horizontal axis represents 'Labor market experience (years)' ranging from 0 to 45 in increments of 5. The vertical axis represents 'Regression error' ranging from -1.0 to 1.0 in increments of 0.5. A horizontal dashed line at Regression error = 0.0 cuts through the center of the contour lines. The concentric contour lines show a bimodal or elongated joint distribution centered vertically around 0.0, spanning roughly between 2 and 43 years of experience, with two peaks: one smaller peak around 10 to 15 years of experience and a higher density peak around 25 to 30 years of experience.

pg_21__page_54_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side by side displaying projections of log wage (in log dollars per hour) against education and labor market experience.

Graph (a) 'Projections onto education':
- X-axis: Education (years), ranging from 4 to 20.
- Y-axis: Log dollars per hour, ranging from 2.0 to 4.0.
- Data points (black dots) are plotted for various years of education.
- Two fitted models are shown: a dashed line for 'Linear projection' (a straight line starting around y = 1.8 at x = 2 and extending up to y = 3.9 at x = 20) and a solid line for 'Linear spline' (which stays relatively flat around y = 2.4 between 4 and 9 years, then bends upward steeply from 10 to 20 years, closely fitting the data points).

Graph (b) 'Projections onto experience':
- X-axis: Labor market experience (years), ranging from 0 to 50.
- Y-axis: Log dollars per hour, ranging from 2.0 to 4.0.
- Three models are plotted:
  1. 'Linear projection': A nearly flat, slightly upward-sloping straight line starting around y = 2.9 at x = 0 and reaching about y = 3.25 at x = 50.
  2. 'Quadratic projection': A smooth downward-concave parabola starting around y = 2.5 at x = 0, peaking near y = 3.1 around 25-30 years of experience, and falling to y = 2.7 at 50 years.
  3. 'Conditional expectation': A curve starting lower (around y = 2.25 at x = 0), rising steeply to meet and closely mirror the quadratic projection from around 10 to 50 years of experience.

pg_21__page_63_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot illustrating the difference between a nonlinear conditional expectation function and two different linear projections. The horizontal axis is labeled 'Regressor' and the vertical axis is labeled 'Dependent variable'. A thick curved line represents the 'Conditional expectation', which starts steep near the origin and flattens out as the regressor increases. Two straight thin lines represent linear projections labeled 'Linear projection 1' (a flatter line with a higher y-intercept) and 'Linear projection 2' (a steeper line with a lower y-intercept), both approximating the curve across different regions.

pg_21__page_66_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A line plot titled 'FIGURE 2.8 Average causal effect vs. regression' displaying 'Wage' on the vertical y-axis (ranging from 8 to 20 in steps of 2) against education level on the horizontal x-axis ('High school' and 'College'). Data points are represented by black circles of varying sizes at High school (at values 8 and 10) and College (at values 12 and 20). Two lines connect the High school region to the College region: the line labeled 'Regression' goes from approximately 8.75 at High school to 17 at College, while the line labeled 'Av. causal effect' has a slightly less steep slope, going from 9 at High school to 16 at College.

pg_21__page_80_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side plots illustrating linear regression with one regressor.

Graph (a), titled '(a) Deviation from fitted line', shows a scatter plot of data points in an X-Y coordinate system with a straight fitted regression line passing through them. Vertical lines connect each data point (represented by small circles) to the fitted line, representing the residuals or deviations from the fitted line.

Graph (b), titled '(b) Sum of squared errors function', shows a parabolic curve plotting the 'Sum of squared errors' (SSE) on the vertical axis against the 'Coefficient' (beta) on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis ranges from 10 to 18, and the horizontal axis ranges from 2.0 to 4.0. The curve reaches a distinct global minimum at approximately Coefficient = 3.1 and SSE = 12, marked by a black dot labeled with beta-hat.

pg_21__page_81_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A 3D scatter plot depicting a multiple linear regression model with two predictor variables, X1 and X2, and a dependent variable, Y. The graph shows a three-dimensional coordinate system with axes labeled Y (vertical axis), X1 (bottom-right horizontal axis), and X2 (depth axis extending upward and to the right). A two-dimensional regression plane is fitted through a cloud of data points (represented as small circles). Vertical line segments (residuals) connect each data point to the regression plane, illustrating the vertical distances between the observed values of Y and the predicted values on the fitted surface.

pg_21__page_81_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A 3D surface plot representing a sum of squared errors (SSE) loss landscape as a function of two regression parameters, beta_1 and beta_2. The vertical z-axis represents the SSE values ranging from 420 to 470. The two horizontal axes represent beta_1 and beta_2, both plotted from 2.0 to 4.0. The surface forms a smooth, bowl-shaped parabolic curve with a distinct global minimum near the center at beta_1 approximately equal to 3.0 and beta_2 approximately equal to 3.0, illustrating how least squares optimization finds the optimal parameter values that minimize error.

pg_21__page_81_Figure_6.jpeg.description:
Figure 3.3 shows two graphs illustrating the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) function with two regressors, beta_1 and beta_2.

Graph (a) on the left displays a 3D surface plot of the SSE function shaped as a parabolic bowl centered over the parameter space. The axes shown are beta_1 ranging from 2.0 to 3.0 and beta_2 ranging from 2.0 to 4.0, showing the minimum of the SSE surface at the bottom of the bowl.

Graph (b) on the right shows a 2D contour plot corresponding to the SSE function. The horizontal axis represents beta_1 (ranging from 2.5 to 4.0) and the vertical axis represents beta_2 (ranging from 2.5 to 3.5). Concentric elliptical contours represent constant levels of SSE, surrounding a central point marked with a dot labeled beta-hat, representing the least squares estimates that minimize the SSE.

pg_21__page_93_Picture_2.jpeg.description: A geometric vector diagram showing a 3D projection corresponding to linear regression with two predictor variables, X_1 and X_2. The vectors X_1 and X_2 form a two-dimensional shaded plane (the column space of the design matrix X). The vector Y extends upward out of this plane from the origin. The orthogonal projection of vector Y onto the X_1-X_2 plane is labeled Y-hat (Ŷ), depicted by a dashed line in the plane starting from the origin and ending at a right-angle perpendicular under the tip of Y. The residual vector, connecting the tip of Y-hat on the plane directly up to the tip of vector Y, is represented by a vertical dashed line labeled e-hat (ê).

pg_21__page_100_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A scatter plot illustrating the impact of an influential observation on Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression lines. The vertical axis is labeled Y and the horizontal axis is labeled X. A cluster of open-circle data points trends upward from lower-left to upper-right. A single filled black circle located at the bottom right (high X, low Y) is pointed to by an arrow and labeled "Influential observation". Two regression lines are drawn: one labeled "Full sample OLS" has a flatter slope pulled downward by the influential observation, while the steeper line labeled "Leave-one-out OLS" shows the regression fit when the single influential observation is excluded.

pg_21__page_120_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled FIGURE 4.1 showing two probability density curves plotted over a horizontal axis representing y. The first curve, labeled f(y), is a wider, symmetric-like distribution with its peak near the center. A vertical arrow points down from the peak of f(y) to a point labeled \beta_0 on the horizontal axis. The second curve, labeled f_\beta(y), is shifted to the right and narrower, with a higher peak. A vertical arrow points down from the peak of f_\beta(y) to a point labeled \beta on the horizontal axis, located to the right of \beta_0.

pg_173__page_2_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two graphs labeled (a) Normal density and (b) Normal distribution, corresponding to the standard normal distribution.

Graph (a) shows the standard normal probability density function, phi(x), plotted on a symmetric bell-shaped curve centered at x = 0 with a peak at y = 0.4. The horizontal axis ranges from -4 to 4, and the vertical axis (density) ranges from 0.0 to 0.4.

nGraph (b) shows the cumulative distribution function, Capital Phi(x), plotted as a smooth S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. The horizontal axis ranges from -4 to 4, and the vertical axis (probability) ranges from 0.0 to 1.0. The curve passes through y = 0.5 at x = 0, approaches 0 as x goes to -4, and approaches 1.0 as x goes to 4.

pg_173__page_29_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled FIGURE 7.1 showing 'The least squares estimator as a function of sample size'. The y-axis is labeled 'Coefficient estimate' ranging from 0.110 to 0.125. The x-axis is labeled 'Number of observations' with tick marks at 5000, 10000, 15000, and 20000. The plotted line, representing the estimator beta_hat_n, fluctuates widely at small numbers of observations (below 2500, swinging between 0.110 and above 0.128) and gradually stabilizes and converges toward approximately 0.113 to 0.114 as the sample size increases toward 20000 and beyond.

pg_173__page_32_Figure_9.jpeg.description:
Figure 7.2 displays two subplots comparing probability density curves of the normalized OLS estimator against the standard normal distribution N(0,1).

Subplot (a), titled '(a) Double pareto error', plots the density across x-axis values from -2 to 2. It shows five curves corresponding to different values of alpha: alpha = 2.05 (dot-dash line with the highest peak at x = 0), alpha = 2.1 (dotted line), alpha = 2.2 (dashed line), alpha = 2.4 (long-dashed line), and N(0,1) (solid line with the lowest peak at x = 0). As alpha decreases toward 2, the density peak around zero becomes progressively taller and sharper, deviating more significantly from the standard normal curve.

Subplot (b), titled '(b) Error process (7.12)', plots the density for different error distributions: N(0,1)^8 (dashed line with the highest, sharply peaked curve around x = -0.5), N(0,1)^6 (dot-dash line), N(0,1)^4 (dotted line), and N(0,1) (solid line). As the exponent increases, the distributions become increasingly skewed and peaked compared to the benchmark standard normal N(0,1) curve.

pg_173__page_33_Figure_11.jpeg.description:
Figure 7.3 shows two side-by-side contour plots illustrating the joint asymptotic probability distribution of parameter estimators beta_1 and beta_2 centered at (0,0):

- Left plot, labeled '(a) Homoskedastic case': Features elliptical contour lines tilted along a negative diagonal slope (top-left to bottom-right). This orientation reflects a negative correlation between beta_1 and beta_2 when regressors are positively correlated under homoskedasticity.
- Right plot, labeled '(b) Heteroskedastic case': Displays horizontally aligned concentric elliptical contours centered at (0,0), demonstrating how heteroskedasticity alters the orientation and correlation structure of the joint distribution.

Both subplots share x-axes labeled beta_1 ranging from -3 to 3 and y-axes labeled beta_2 ranging from -3 to 3.

pg_173__page_48_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side labeled Figure 7.4 'Regression intervals', displaying estimated non-linear relationships with confidence bands shaded in grey.

Chart (a) 'Wage on education': The x-axis represents 'Education (years)' ranging from 6 to 20. The y-axis represents 'Log wage' ranging from 1.0 to 4.0. A nearly linear black solid line shows a positive relationship starting around (6, 1.6) and rising to (20, 3.8). A grey shaded confidence interval band surrounds the line, which is wider at lower values of education (around 6 years) and narrower around 16–18 years.

Chart (b) 'Wage on experience': The x-axis represents 'Experience (years)' ranging from 0 to 60. The y-axis represents 'Log wage' ranging from 2.2 to 2.8. A concave black solid line starts around (0, 2.36), peaks between 30 and 40 years of experience at approximately 2.64, and then declines toward 2.50 at 60 years. The grey shaded confidence interval band is tightest around the middle range (20–40 years) and flares significantly wider at both extremes (0 years and 60 years).

pg_173__page_52_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional scatter plot showing a confidence region for two parameters: 'Return to education (%)' on the horizontal x-axis and 'Return to experience (%)' on the vertical y-axis. The x-axis ranges from 10 to 14 in increments of 1. The y-axis ranges from 0.0 to 2.5 in increments of 0.5. Inside the plot, a shaded gray elliptical confidence region spans approximately from 10.1 to 13.5 on the x-axis and 0.3 to 2.0 on the y-axis, tilted slightly upwards to the right. Near the center of the ellipse, at approximately x = 11.8, y = 1.1, there is a black dot labeled with the point estimate symbol beta-hat (β̂).

pg_173__page_63_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A contour plot illustrating the constrained least squares criterion on a two-dimensional parameter space with axes labeled $\beta_1$ on the horizontal axis and $\beta_2$ on the vertical axis, both ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. A straight diagonal constraint boundary line runs from $(0.0, 1.0)$ to $(1.0, 0.0)$, forming a triangular feasible region bounded by the coordinate axes and this diagonal line. Inside the region, concentric elliptical contours represent the sum-of-squares loss function. The center point of these contours is labeled $\hat{\beta}_{ols}$ (unconstrained ordinary least squares estimate) located around $(0.33, 0.27)$. The point where the outermost depicted elliptical contour is tangent to the diagonal constraint line is labeled $\tilde{\beta}_{cls}$ (constrained least squares estimate) located around $(0.52, 0.48)$.

pg_173__page_88_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two circular diagrams illustrating hypothesis testing concepts. 

Diagram (a) is titled "Null and alternative hypotheses". It shows a large circle representing the parameter space, labeled $H_1$ in the outer region, with a smaller concentric circle inside labeled $H_0$, illustrating the null hypothesis as a subset of the entire space.

Diagram (b) is titled "Acceptance and rejection regions". It shows a circle split horizontally by a wavy boundary line into two regions. The top region is labeled $T < c$ and $S_0$ (representing the acceptance region), while the bottom region is labeled $T > c$ and $S_1$ (representing the rejection region).

pg_173__page_105_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A line plot titled 'FIGURE 9.2 Wald statistic as a function of s' showing two curves representing the Wald statistic on the y-axis (ranging from 0 to 5) plotted against parameter 's' on the x-axis (ranging from 1 to 10).

1. Decreasing curve labeled 'beta = 1.6': Starts around a Wald statistic value of 3.6 at s = 1, decreases nonlinearly as s increases, passing through approximately 1.0 at s = 4.6, and approaches approximately 0.25 at s = 10.
2. Increasing curve labeled 'beta = 0.8': Starts near a Wald statistic value of 0.4 at s = 1, increases nonlinearly as s increases, intersecting the other curve near (4.6, 1.0), and reaches approximately 4.4 at s = 10.

pg_173__page_114_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 9.3 shows two side-by-side plots illustrating asymptotic local power functions:

(a) One-sided t-test: Plots Power (from 0.0 to 1.0) against parameter delta (from -1 to 4). Two sigmoid curves are shown for alpha = 0.05 and alpha = 0.1. A horizontal dashed line at Power = 0.5 intersects both curves, and vertical dashed indicators highlight specific power levels at delta = 1.

(b) Vector case: Plots Power (from 0.0 to 1.0) against non-centrality parameter lambda (from 0 to 8). Three upward-sloping curves represent different values of q (q = 1, q = 2, and q = 3). A horizontal dashed line at Power = 0.5 intersects all three curves, showing that higher values of q require a larger lambda to achieve the same power level.

pg_173__page_132_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 10.1 shows two probability density distribution plots representing bootstrap distributions.

Graph (a) titled 'Return to education' plots a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution. A dashed vertical line marks the peak at approximately 0.155. Arrows pointing down to the x-axis mark the tails of the distribution around 0.08 and 0.215. The x-axis ranges from 0.00 to 0.30 in increments of 0.05.

Graph (b) titled 'Mean wage of college graduates' plots a slightly right-skewed bell-shaped distribution. A dashed vertical line marks the peak at approximately 25.8. Arrows pointing down to the x-axis mark the lower and upper bounds around 21.5 and 30.7. The x-axis ranges from 15 to 35 in increments of 5.

pg_321__page_57_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two plots illustrating examples of endogeneity, titled Figure 12.1: Examples of endogeneity.

Left Plot (a) Measurement error:
- Shows a scatter plot with 'Regressor' on the horizontal axis (values 1 to 7) and 'Dependent variable' on the vertical axis (values 1 to 3).
- Data points include filled circles and open circles.
- Two regression lines are plotted:
  1. A steeper line labeled 'No measurement error' passing through the filled circles at points (2,1), (4,2), and (6,3).
  2. A flatter line labeled 'With measurement error' fitting both sets of points, demonstrating attenuation bias caused by measurement error in the regressor.

Right Plot (b) Supply and demand:
- Shows a market equilibrium framework with 'Price' on the horizontal axis (values 1 to 3) and 'Quantity' on the vertical axis (values 1 to 3).
- An upward-sloping line is labeled 'Supply' and a downward-sloping line is labeled 'Demand', intersecting at Price = 2, Quantity = 2.
- Four data points are plotted around the equilibrium: (1,2), (2,3), (3,2), and (2,1).
- A flat horizontal line labeled 'Regression' passes through Quantity = 2, illustrating simultaneous equations bias (endogeneity) where standard OLS regression fails to estimate either the supply or demand curve.

pg_471__page_20_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Four line plots arranged in a two-by-two grid displaying historical U.S. economic time series from 1960 to nearly 2020:

(a) U.S. real GDP: Plotted in trillions of chained 2012 dollars on the y-axis (ranging from 4 to 18) against time on the x-axis. It shows a strong, steady upward trend from around 3 trillion in 1960 to over 18 trillion by 2018, with slight dips during economic recessions (e.g., around 2008).

(b) U.S.-Canada exchange rate: Plotted in Canadian dollar per U.S. dollar on the y-axis (ranging from 1.0 to 1.6). It starts around 1.0 in 1960, rises to peak near 1.6 around 2002, drops back to around 1.0 near 2010, and then fluctuates back up toward 1.4.

(c) Interest rate on 10-year treasury: Plotted as a percentage on the y-axis (ranging from 2 to 14). It rises from around 4% in 1960 to a high peak of over 14% around 1980–1982, followed by a sustained downward trend reaching under 2% by 2018.

(d) Real crude oil price: Plotted in 2012 dollars per barrel on the y-axis (ranging from 0 to 120). It remains low and flat (under $20) through the 1960s and 1970s, spikes in the late 1970s/early 1980s, drops through the 1990s, and experiences extreme volatility after 2000, peaking above $120 around 2008 before dropping sharply and fluctuating.

pg_471__page_21_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Four line plots arranged in a two-by-two grid displaying monthly U.S. macroeconomic and financial time series from 1960 to 2020:

(a) U.S. unemployment rate (top-left): A percentage line chart showing cyclical fluctuations with distinct peaks above 8% or 10% around 1975, 1982-1983, and 2008-2010, ranging between roughly 3.5% and 10.8%.

(b) Consumption growth rate (top-right): A percentage line chart depicting a stationary, highly volatile series centered near 0.5% to 1%, ranging mostly between -2% and 3.5%.

(c) U.S. inflation rate (bottom-left): A percentage line chart with higher level and volatility during the 1970s and early 1980s (peaking near 1.8%), stabilization at lower levels (0% to 0.5%) after 1990, and notable sharp drops (down to -0.8%) during the 2008 financial crisis.

(d) S&P 500 return (bottom-right): A percentage line chart showing high-frequency stock return fluctuations centered around 0% with extreme negative spikes down to -12% to -18% (e.g., around October 1987 and late 2008).

pg_471__page_40_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side comparing a time series of white noise against a moving average MA(8) process from 1990 to 2015.

Chart (a), labeled "White noise", shows a highly erratic, rapidly fluctuating line centered around 0, with values ranging primarily between -2 and 2.

Chart (b), labeled "MA(8)", shows a much smoother, wave-like time series with longer-term cycles, fluctuating between values of -8 and 6 over the same period.

pg_471__page_41_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side comparing two AR(1) time series processes over the years 1990 to 2015.

Chart (a), labeled "(a) AR(1) with \alpha_1 = 0.5", shows a stationary process oscillating rapidly around a mean of 0, with values ranging primarily between -3 and 3.

Chart (b), labeled "(b) AR(1) with \alpha_1 = 0.95", demonstrates much higher persistence and smoother, longer waves, wandering further away from the mean with values ranging from approximately -7 to 5.

pg_471__page_45_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 14.5 consists of two side-by-side line charts illustrating random walk processes over the period from 1985 to 2015.

- Subfigure (a) labeled '(a) Example 1': Displays a time series plot fluctuating roughly between -9 and +6. The process shows distinct cyclical upward and downward trends over time, peaking around 1991 near 6 and reaching a trough around 2006 near -9, before recovering toward -2 by 2015.

- Subfigure (b) labeled '(b) Example 2': Displays a time series plot starting near 0 around 1985–1993, followed by a sharp downward trend between 1995 and 2000 that drops the value to around -25. From 2000 to 2015, the series stabilizes and fluctuates horizontally between -22 and -30.

pg_471__page_47_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A triangular stationarity region plot for a second-order autoregressive AR(2) process, plotted on axes of \alpha_1 (horizontal axis, ranging from -2 to 2) and \alpha_2 (vertical axis, ranging from -1.5 to 1.0). The triangular region is bounded by three straight lines: the bottom horizontal line at \alpha_2 = -1, the top-left boundary defined by \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 = 1, and the top-right boundary defined by \alpha_1 - \alpha_2 = 1. Inside the triangle, a curved boundary (a downward-opening parabola starting from (-2, -1), reaching a peak at (0, 0), and ending at (2, -1)) divides the region into two sections: 'Real factors' in the upper region above the curve, and 'Complex factors' in the lower region below the curve.

pg_471__page_48_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 14.7 consists of two side-by-side line graphs comparing different AR(2) processes over time from approximately 1987 to 2015.

Graph (a), labeled "(a) AR(2)", shows a time series plot where values fluctuate between -4 and 3 over time, exhibiting persistent trends and smooth, broader swings across the years.

Graph (b), labeled "(b) AR(2) with complex roots", shows a time series plot fluctuating between -4 and 6, displaying a distinct, more regular pseudo-cyclical oscillation pattern throughout the sample period.

pg_471__page_105_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side showing the dynamic response of GDP growth to an orthogonalized Federal Funds shock over a 20-quarter horizon, with gray shaded confidence bands surrounding the central estimate lines.

Chart (a), titled '(a) Impulse response function', plots quarterly response starting near 0.0 at quarter 0, rising slightly, then sharply dipping to around -0.22 at quarter 2, before fluctuating upward and returning close to 0.0 by quarter 10-12 and remaining slightly above zero through quarter 20. A dashed horizontal reference line is set at 0.0.

Chart (b), titled '(b) Cumulative IRF', plots the cumulative response starting near 0.0 at quarter 0, declining sharply to around -0.65 by quarter 8, and then slowly recovering towards roughly -0.38 by quarter 20. A dashed horizontal reference line is set at 0.0.

pg_471__page_109_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two impulse response function line charts titled '(a) Supply shock' and '(b) Aggregate demand shock', depicting the response of oil prices over a horizon of 0 to 24 months.

- Subplot (a) Supply shock: Shows the oil price response rising slightly to a peak around month 4 (near 1.3), then steadily declining back down toward zero around month 20, dropping slightly below zero by month 24. A gray shaded area represents the confidence band around the central line.
- Subplot (b) Aggregate demand shock: Shows a continuous upward trajectory from month 0 to month 24, starting near 0.4 and reaching approximately 4.7 by month 24. The gray confidence band widens significantly over time, remaining entirely above zero from around month 6 onward.

Both plots have horizontal axes labeled 'Months' with ticks at 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24, and vertical axes ranging from -2 to 8. A dashed horizontal line indicates zero response.

pg_471__page_112_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two impulse response function plots showing the response of GDP over 16 quarters, labeled (a) Spending and (b) Taxes. Both plots have Quarters on the horizontal axis ranging from 0 to 16 (marked at 0, 4, 8, 12, 16) and vertical axis values ranging from -0.8 to 0.8 in increments of 0.4, with a dashed reference line at 0.0.

Plot (a) Spending shows a positive response of GDP, starting around 0.2 at quarter 0, rising slightly to approximately 0.25 around quarter 4, and stabilizing near 0.25 through quarter 16. A shaded 95% confidence interval band spans roughly 0.1 to 0.3 at quarter 0 and widens to approximately -0.1 to 0.57 by quarter 16.

Plot (b) Taxes shows a negative response of GDP to a tax shock, starting at around -0.17 at quarter 0, dipping further to approximately -0.48 around quarters 5-7, and then gradually recovering toward -0.17 by quarter 16. The shaded confidence interval band spans roughly -0.08 to -0.3 at quarter 0, dipping as low as -0.8 at quarter 6, and ending between -0.5 and 0.15 at quarter 16.

pg_471__page_116_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side by side displaying impulse response functions for unemployment rate over 24 quarters following economic shocks, titled FIGURE 15.4. 

Panel (a), labeled '(a) Supply shock', plots the response of the unemployment rate over 0 to 24 quarters following a supply shock. It starts near 0.0 at quarter 0, rises to a peak of approximately 0.35 around quarter 5, and then gradually declines back toward 0.0 by quarter 24. A gray shaded region represents the confidence interval band, which peaks around 0.6 near quarter 5 and tapers off toward quarter 24.

Panel (b), labeled '(b) Demand shock', plots the response of the unemployment rate over 0 to 24 quarters following a demand shock. It starts around 0.22 at quarter 0, rises to a peak of around 0.42 near quarter 4, and gradually decays toward 0.0 by quarter 24. The gray confidence interval band starts around 0.2 to 0.4 at quarter 0, peaks around 0.57 at quarter 4, and tapers down toward quarter 24.

pg_471__page_117_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 15.5 consists of two side-by-side line graphs showing the forecast error variance decomposition (percent due to a supply shock) over a horizon of 24 quarters.

- Subplot (a) titled '(a) GDP' displays the proportion of GDP forecast error variance explained by the supply shock. It starts at 0 at quarter 0, sharply jumps to around 0.83 at quarter 1, slightly drops to approximately 0.77 around quarter 2, and then remains nearly flat around 0.77 through quarter 24. A shaded region around the central line represents the confidence band, ranging roughly from 0.41 to 1.0 after quarter 2.

- Subplot (b) titled '(b) Unemployment rate' shows the proportion of unemployment rate forecast error variance attributable to the supply shock. It starts at 0 at quarter 0, rises smoothly to about 0.25 at quarter 4, 0.38 at quarter 8, and plateaus around 0.42 from quarter 12 to 24. A shaded confidence band expands over time, spanning from approximately 0.0 to 0.83 at quarter 24.

Both plots have an x-axis labeled 'Quarters' marked from 0 to 24 in increments of 4, and a y-axis ranging from 0.0 to 1.0 in increments of 0.2.

pg_471__page_132_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 16.1 consists of two line graphs, labeled (a) and (b), plotting a time series generated by a random walk from t = 0 to t = 240, with values ranging from -10 to 8.

Graph (a) titled '(a) Fitted means' displays three horizontal dashed lines over the time series line plot:
- 'Sample mean': a dashed line spanning the entire time axis at approximately y = -3.
- 'Mean, t ≤ 120': a dashed line spanning from t = 0 to t = 120 at approximately y = -0.8, with an arrow pointing down to it.
- 'Mean, t > 120': a dashed line spanning from t = 120 to t = 240 at approximately y = -5.2, with an arrow pointing down to it.

Graph (b) titled '(b) Fitted trend' displays the exact same time series with a single straight downward-sloping dashed line labeled 'Fitted trend', starting near y = 2.3 at t = 0 and decreasing linearly to around y = -8.3 at t = 240.

pg_471__page_135_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side line plots showing detrended random walk time series data across 240 time steps.

Graph (a), titled '(a) Linearly detrended series', plots values ranging from -6 to 8 on the vertical axis against time steps from 0 to 240 on the horizontal axis. A dashed horizontal reference line is set at y = 0. The series displays cyclic fluctuations, peaking near y = 8 around step 50 and near y = 6 around step 165, with major troughs reaching below -4 around steps 85 and 110.

Graph (b), titled '(b) First difference detrended series', plots a similar series over the same range (0 to 240 time steps and values from -5 to 9). It shows comparable cyclic patterns with a horizontal dashed reference line at y = 0, peaking near y = 9 around step 50 and y = 6 around step 165, and dropping to troughs below -4 near steps 85, 110, and 195.

pg_471__page_138_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two graphs illustrating unit root distributions under three different specifications: 'No intercept', 'Intercept', and 'Trend'.

Graph (a) labeled '(a) Dickey-Fuller coefficient density' shows three probability density curves plotted against values ranging from -30 to 0 on the horizontal axis:
1. 'No intercept': A very sharp, high peak centered close to 0.
2. 'Intercept': A broader, moderately high distribution shifted to the left, peaking around -3.
3. 'Trend': The widest distribution with a lower peak, shifted furthest to the left and centered around -7, with a long tail extending toward -30.

Graph (b) labeled '(b) Dickey-Fuller T density' shows three bell-shaped t-statistic density curves plotted against values ranging from -5 to 3 on the horizontal axis:
1. 'No intercept': Centered furthest to the right with its peak near -0.7.
2. 'Intercept': Shifted slightly left, with its peak near -1.5.
3. 'Trend': Shifted furthest to the left, with its peak near -2.1.

pg_471__page_147_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled FIGURE 16.4 showing the probability density functions of the KPSS distribution for two cases, labeled KPSS1 and KPSS2. The horizontal axis represents values ranging from 0.0 to 0.5 with tick marks at intervals of 0.1. The distribution for KPSS1 has a lower peak occurring near 0.06 and a right-skewed, heavy tail extending toward 0.5. The distribution for KPSS2 is sharper with a significantly higher peak near 0.04 and a faster decay, reaching near zero around 0.2.

pg_471__page_149_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side time series plots labeled (a) and (b) illustrating spurious regression patterns:

- Subfigure (a), titled "(a) Two unrelated random walks", shows two time series plotted from 1980 to 2020:
  - "Series 1" (dashed line) starts around 1980, trends upward with fluctuations, drops around 2000, peaks sharply around 2012, and then declines toward 2020.
  - "Series 2" (solid line) trends upward continuously from 1980, peaks around 2007, drops slightly, and tracks near Series 1 through 2020.

- Subfigure (b), titled "(b) Exchange and labor force participation rates", plots two economic series from 1960 to 2020:
  - "Participation rate" (dashed line) rises steadily from 1960, peaks around 2000, and declines gradually through 2020.
  - "Exchange rate" (solid line) shows a plateau in the 1960s, rises steeply through 1980 to a peak around 2000, then undergoes sharp volatility and declines significantly after 2000, before partially rebounding toward 2020.

pg_621__page_0_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 16.6 shows two plots illustrating properties of spurious regression.

Graph (a) labeled "Asymptotic density of sample correlation": Plots a symmetric, inverted U-shaped probability density curve spanning from -1.0 to 1.0 on the horizontal axis. The curve rises sharply near -1.0, flattens out into a wide plateau around 0.0, and drops sharply near 1.0.

Graph (b) labeled "Coverage probability of nominal 95% interval": Plots Probability on the vertical axis (from 0.0 to 0.6) against Sample size on the horizontal axis (from 0 to 200). The curve starts high near a probability above 0.6 at very small sample sizes and decreases monotonically as sample size increases, dropping below 0.2 by sample size 200.

pg_621__page_4_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side line graphs showing U.S. interest rate data from 1960 to nearly 2020.

Left plot (a) 'Interest rates': Plots two lines representing percentage rates over time from 1960 to around 2018. The solid line represents the '10-year rate', and the dashed line represents the '3-month rate'. Both series rise from around 3-4% in 1960 to a high peak around 14-15% in the early 1980s, followed by a steady downward trend toward 0-3% by 2010-2018. The two series track each other closely throughout the time period.

Right plot (b) 'Interest rate spread': Plots the difference (spread) between the 10-year rate and 3-month rate over the same period (1960 to nearly 2020), with values on the vertical axis ranging from -2 to 4 percent. A horizontal dashed line indicates the mean level around 1.5%. The spread fluctuates continuously around this mean, dipping below 0% (negative spread / yield curve inversion) around 1970, 1974, 1980, 1981, 1989, 2000, and 2007, and peaking above 3% multiple times.

pg_621__page_6_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A scatter plot titled 'FIGURE 16.8 Error correction effect' illustrating the relationship between the 10-year interest rate (x-axis, ranging from 0 to 16) and the 3-month interest rate (y-axis, ranging from 0 to 16).

Key components:
- Numerous open circles represent data points clustered along an upward-sloping diagonal trendline running from approximately (2, 0.5) to (16, 14.5).
- Four solid black dots represent extreme or off-equilibrium data points, each accompanied by an arrow pointing toward the main concentration of data along the trendline:
  1. A solid dot at roughly x = 4, y = 8 with an arrow pointing down and right towards the main cluster.
  2. A solid dot at roughly x = 8, y = 13 with an arrow pointing down and right towards the main cluster.
  3. A solid dot at roughly x = 10, y = 4 with an arrow pointing up and left towards the main cluster.
  4. A solid dot at roughly x = 14, y = 7 with an arrow pointing up and left towards the main cluster.

pg_621__page_35_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A scatter plot illustrating a pooled ordinary least squares regression (least squares fit) vs. individual firm relationships (true regression lines). The vertical axis represents Y, and the horizontal axis represents X. A long, upward-sloping solid line labeled 'Least squares fit' passes through three clusters of data points corresponding to three different firms: 'Firm 1' (represented by square markers at lower X and Y values), 'Firm 2' (represented by circle markers at intermediate X and Y values), and 'Firm 3' (represented by triangle markers at high X and Y values). For each firm, the short line segment connecting its data points slopes downward (negative slope), labeled 'True regression line'. This illustrates Simpson's Paradox / aggregation bias, where the overall pooled regression line has a positive slope despite every individual firm having a negative relationship between X and Y.

pg_621__page_93_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A line plot titled 'FIGURE 18.1 Liquor sales by state' displaying the log per capita sales of liquor from 1970 to 2007 for three states: New York, California, and Iowa.

- Vertical Axis: Log per capita sales, ranging from -0.6 to 0.4 in increments of 0.2.
- Horizontal Axis: Years from 1970 to 2000 in increments of 10 years, extending to around 2007.
- New York & California lines: Both start near 0.4 in 1970 and show a steep, steady decline through the 1980s and early 1990s, reaching minimum levels between -0.4 and -0.7 around 1995, before moderately increasing through 2007.
- Iowa line: Starts lower around -0.25 in 1970, slightly rises to -0.15 by the mid-1970s, then declines sharply into the late 1980s and early 1990s reaching below -0.7, followed by a steady upward trend back toward -0.3 by 2007.

pg_621__page_102_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side scatter plots with overlaid non-parametric regression curves showing dependent variable versus regressor (0 to 10).

Left Plot (a) Nadaraya-Watson:
- Shows scatter data points alongside three curves/lines: Binned Means (dashed horizontal segments with square markers at bin midpoints x=1, 3, 5, 7, 9), Rolling Binned (solid line moving continuously across the domain), and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression (dash-dotted line).
- Vertical dotted lines mark bin boundaries at x=0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
- The curves peak around x=2 to 2.5 near y=1.0 and descend to around y=-0.1 for x >= 7.

Right Plot (b) Local Linear:
- Shows the same scatter data with three curves: Binned Regression (dashed line segments with slopes inside each bin), Rolling Binned (solid line), and Local Linear regression (dash-dotted line).
- Unlike the Nadaraya-Watson estimator on the left which flattens out near boundaries, the Local Linear estimator handles boundary slopes and trends without flattening bias.

pg_621__page_108_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled FIGURE 19.2 'Smoothing bias' showing the relationship between a regressor on the x-axis (ranging from 0 to 10) and a dependent variable on the y-axis (ranging from -0.5 to 1.5). The graph illustrates four curves representing a true regression function m(x) and three smoothed estimators with different bandwidth values h: h = 1/2, h = 1, and h = 3/2. The solid line represents m(x), reaching a peak near y = 1.0 at x = 2 and a trough near y = -0.2 at x = 8. As bandwidth h increases, the curves become progressively flatter and smoothed out, demonstrating how larger bandwidths reduce variance but introduce smoothing bias near peaks and troughs.

pg_621__page_112_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A scatter plot illustrating boundary bias in Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression. The horizontal axis is labeled 'Regressor' ranging from 0 to 10. The vertical axis is labeled 'Dependent variable' ranging from -2 to 12. A solid straight line represents the true regression function m(x), running from (0, 0) to (10, 10). Scatter points (data observations) are distributed along this line with random noise. Two Nadaraya-Watson estimators are plotted: one with bandwidth h=1 (dashed line) and one with bandwidth h=2 (short-dashed/dotted line). Both non-parametric lines show significant boundary bias near the endpoints x=0 and x=10, where the estimated curves flatten and deviate away from the true linear relationship m(x) towards the center of the data distribution.

pg_621__page_117_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two-panel figure labeled 'FIGURE 19.4 Bandwidth selection'.

Panel (a) 'Cross-validation criterion': Shows a plot of the cross-validation criterion versus bandwidth (ranging from 0.2 to 1.6). Two U-shaped curves are plotted: a dashed curve representing 'CV(h), Nadaraya-Watson' with a minimum near bandwidth 0.83, and a solid curve representing 'CV(h), Local Linear' with a lower minimum near bandwidth 0.77. Vertical arrows indicate the minimizing bandwidth values for each method.

Panel (b) 'Nonparametric estimates': Shows a scatter plot of data points (Dependent variable vs. Regressor, from 0 to 10). Three curves are fitted to the data: a solid curve representing the true or underlying function m(x), a short-dashed curve representing h_ROT (rule-of-thumb bandwidth estimate), and a long-dashed curve representing h_CV (cross-validation bandwidth estimate). Both bandwidth estimates trace the non-linear sinusoidal-like trend of the data points closely.

pg_621__page_122_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 19.5 consists of two side-by-side plots labeled (a) and (b):

(a) Plot titled '(a) Cross-validation criterion': The y-axis represents the 'Cross-validation criterion' ranging from 0.2295 to 0.2310. The x-axis represents 'Bandwidth' ranging from 2 to 11. A U-shaped curve reaches its minimum value near a bandwidth of 4.3, marked with a point labeled 'h_CV'.

(b) Plot titled '(b) Local Linear regression': The y-axis represents 'Log wage' ranging from 2.0 to 2.7. The x-axis represents 'Experience (years)' from 0 to 40. Two overlapping fitted lines are shown: a solid line representing 'h_ROT' and a dashed line representing 'h_CV'. Both lines show log wage rising sharply from around 2.2 at 0 years of experience up to a peak near 2.58 around 23-25 years of experience, followed by a slight decline and leveling off around 2.57 through 40 years.

pg_621__page_123_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
The image consists of two side-by-side plots labeled (a) and (b).

Plot (a) is titled "Cross-validation for conditional variance". The vertical axis represents the "Cross-validation criterion" ranging from 1.204 to 1.212. The horizontal axis represents "Bandwidth" ranging from 5 to 40. It shows two curves:
1. "Local Linear": Starts high, drops sharply near bandwidth 5, rises to a local peak around bandwidth 8-9, and then gradually decreases to plateau around 1.209.
2. "Nadaraya-Watson": Starts high, drops continuously, and levels off near 1.203 at higher bandwidth values (around 35-40).

Plot (b) is titled "Regression with Confidence Bands". The vertical axis represents "Log wage" ranging from 2.0 to 2.7. The horizontal axis represents "Experience (years)" from 0 to 40. It displays an estimated curve showing log wage as a function of experience, surrounded by a gray shaded confidence band. The curve starts around a log wage of 2.2 at 0 years of experience, increases steadily to reach a peak around 2.58 at 25 years of experience, slightly drops around 30 years, and then flattens out around 2.58 up to 40 years. The confidence band is wider at the left end (0 years) and right end (35-40 years) and narrower in the middle range (15-30 years).

pg_621__page_125_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 19.7 contains two line plots illustrating bandwidth selection and local linear regression for test scores:

Panel (a) Cross-validation criterion: Plots the Cross-validation criterion on the y-axis (ranging from 0.00 to 0.10) against Bandwidth on the x-axis (ranging from 4 to 20). Two curves are shown: standard CV(h) (dashed line), which reaches a minimum around bandwidth 12 to 13, and Clustered CV(h) (solid line), which dips steeply to a local minimum around bandwidth 6.5 before rising again.

Panel (b) Local Linear regression: Plots Test score on the y-axis (ranging from 0 to 30) against Initial percentile on the x-axis (ranging from 0 to 90). It compares a solid line representing the Local Linear estimate (surrounded by a shaded confidence interval band) with a dashed line representing the Global Linear estimate. Both estimates show a steady positive non-linear relationship between initial percentile and test score, rising from around 6 at the 0th percentile to around 22–26 at the 90th percentile.

pg_621__page_139_Figure_2.jpeg.description: Two side-by-side line plots showing polynomial estimates of the experience profile (Log dollars per hour vs. Experience in years from 0 to 40) for two demographic groups. Graph (a) shows estimates for 'White women', where polynomial fits of degrees 2, 4, 8, and 12 all yield smooth, smooth concave curves peaking around 25 years of experience at a log wage slightly above 3.1. Graph (b) shows estimates for 'Black women', where higher-degree polynomials (8 and 12) exhibit severe overfitting and oscillatory behavior (Runge's phenomenon) near the boundaries (40+ years), while lower-degree polynomials (2 and 4) remain smooth.

pg_621__page_143_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side illustrating spline regression models, labeled as Figure 20.2 Spline regression estimates.

Left Plot: '(a) Experience profile'
- X-axis: Experience (years), ranging from 0 to 40.
- Y-axis: Log dollars per hour, ranging from 2.4 to 3.4.
- Content: Shows a quadratic spline (solid line) and a 6th-degree polynomial (dashed line) fitted to data, both forming an inverted U-shape peaking around 28 to 30 years of experience at roughly 3.26 log dollars per hour. Knots (solid dots) are located at 10, 20, 30, and 40 years along the quadratic spline.

Right Plot: '(b) Effect of income on transfers'
- X-axis: Total income (pesos), ranging from 0 to 200,000.
- Y-axis: Transfers (pesos), ranging from 4,000 to 12,000.
- Content: Shows a linear spline (solid line) with knots (solid dots) at low and higher income levels. The curve drops sharply from over 14,000 pesos at 0 income down to around 7,000 pesos at 20,000 income, then flattens out around 6,000 to 7,000 pesos across higher income levels up to 200,000 pesos.

pg_621__page_144_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line plots showing the kernel representation of a polynomial weight function for different values of x.

Left plot: (a) x = 0.5
- The horizontal axis shows x values from 0.0 to 1.0.
- The vertical axis shows the Kernel function values from -2 to 8.
- Curves are shown for polynomial degrees p = 4 (dashed line), p = 8 (dash-dotted line), and p = 12 (solid line).
- All three curves peak around x = 0.5, with higher values of p producing a taller, narrower, more localized central peak (reaching around 7.3 for p = 12) along with oscillating side lobes.

Right plot: (a) x = 0.25
- The horizontal axis shows x values from 0.0 to 1.0.
- The vertical axis shows the Kernel function values from -4 to 8.
- Curves are shown for p = 4 (dashed line) and p = 12 (solid line).
- The main peak shifts to around x = 0.25. For p = 12, the peak is sharply localized near x = 0.25 (height above 8), with significant oscillations across the domain.

pg_621__page_148_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled 'FIGURE 20.4 Normalized regressor length' comparing 'Polynomial' (solid line) and 'Quadratic spline' (dashed line). The y-axis represents the 'Length of regressor vector' ranging from 0 to 10. The x-axis represents 'x' ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. Both curves show very high values near the boundaries (x = 0 and x = 1), reaching up to 10 for Polynomial and around 7.2 for Quadratic spline. In the middle region (x between 0.1 and 0.9), both curves oscillate at a much lower level around 2.5 to 4.0, with the Quadratic spline displaying slightly larger amplitude oscillations across the interior domain than the Polynomial curve.

pg_771__page_1_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Line plot illustrating integrated squared error against series order (K) ranging from 1 to 8. The vertical axis represents 'Integrated squared error' with values from 0.0 to 1.0, and the horizontal axis represents 'Series order' (K) from 1 to 8.

Three curves corresponding to different error bounds are displayed:
1. Top dashed line labelled K⁻⁴ + K / 10: Drops sharply from 1.0 at K=1 to a local minimum around K=2 (marked with a black dot at approximately ISE = 0.26), then increases steadily up to 0.8 at K=8.
2. Middle dashed line labelled K⁻⁴ + K / 30: Drops sharply from 1.0 at K=1, reaches its minimum around K=3 (marked with a black dot at approximately ISE = 0.11), then increases slowly up to about 0.27 at K=8.
3. Bottom solid line labelled K⁻⁴ + K / 150: Drops sharply from 1.0 at K=1, flattens out to its minimum around K=4 (marked with a black dot at approximately ISE = 0.03), and remains nearly flat up to K=8.

Overall, the figure demonstrates the trade-off between bias (K⁻⁴ term) and variance (K/n term) where larger sample size denominators (10, 30, 150) shift the optimal series order K to higher values and produce lower overall integrated squared error.

pg_771__page_5_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 20.6 shows two line plots comparing the cross-validation criterion CV(K) across different polynomial orders (from 1 to 8) for experience profile estimates:

1. Plot (a) White women: The cross-validation criterion starts around 1260 at polynomial order 1, sharply decreases to around 1227 at order 2, reaches a minimum point marked by a filled dot at order 3 (around 1225), and then gradually increases up to around 1233 at order 8.

2. Plot (b) Black women: The cross-validation criterion starts around 125.2 at polynomial order 1, reaches a minimum point marked by a filled dot at order 2 (around 124.3), stays relatively flat through order 4, increases slightly through orders 5–7, and sharply increases near 130 at order 8.

pg_771__page_8_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side line plots showing polynomial estimates of log hourly earnings based on years of experience, complete with 95% confidence bands (shaded gray regions).

Left plot: '(a) White women'
- X-axis: 'Experience (years)' ranging from 0 to 45 (labeled at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40).
- Y-axis: 'Log dollars per hour' ranging from 2.4 to 3.2.
- The curve starts low at around 2.5 when experience is 0, increases steeply to a peak slightly above 3.1 between 20 and 30 years of experience, and then declines toward 3.0 at 45 years. The confidence band is narrow early on and widens significantly at higher experience levels (above 35 years).

Right plot: '(b) Black women'
- Same axes and ranges as plot (a).
- The curve starts around 2.74 at 0 years of experience, increases smoothly to a peak near 3.1 around 25 to 30 years of experience, and levels off slightly above 3.0 at 45 years. The confidence band is wider overall compared to plot (a), particularly at 0 years and at higher experience levels (above 35 years).

pg_771__page_17_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side line plots showing nonparametric instrumental variables estimates of reading test scores with 95% confidence intervals (shaded regions).

Left Plot: '(a) Effect of classize'
- Vertical axis: 'Reading test score', ranging from 65 to 80.
- Horizontal axis: 'Class size', ranging from 20 to 40.
- Trend: Shows a slight, nearly linear negative relationship. As class size increases from 20 to 40, the reading test score gradually declines from approximately 73.5 to around 70.5.

Right Plot: '(b) Effect of percent disadvantaged'
- Vertical axis: 'Reading test score', ranging from 65 to 80.
- Horizontal axis: 'Percentage disadvantaged', ranging from 0 to 50.
- Trend: Shows a strong, non-linear negative relationship. As the percentage of disadvantaged students increases from 0% to 50%, reading test scores drop significantly from around 80.5 down to 64.

pg_771__page_29_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts illustrating regression discontinuity design (RDD):

(a) Sharp regression discontinuity: Plot of Dependent variable versus Running variable (from 0.0 to 2.5). A vertical line marks the cut-off point 'c' at 1.0, separating regions X < c and X > c. To the left of c, solid curve m_0(x) shows a continuous function extending as a dashed line past c. To the right of c, solid curve m_1(x) represents the shifted function, with a vertical jump of magnitude theta (\theta) occurring at the threshold c.

(b) Effect of head start on childhood mortality: Plot of Mortality rate (1 to 5) versus Poverty rate (20 to 80). A vertical line marks the Cut-off at a poverty rate of 60, dividing the sample into 'Untreated' (below 60) and 'Treated' (60 and above). The mortality rate increases with poverty rate up to nearly 3.3 just before 60, then sharply drops to around 1.8 immediately after the cut-off, with shaded regions indicating confidence intervals.

pg_771__page_35_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two diagnostic charts for Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), labeled (a) and (b).

Graph (a), titled '(a) RDD with covariates':
- X-axis: Poverty rate, ranging from 20 to 80 with increments of 10.
- Y-axis: Mortality rate, ranging from 1 to 5.
- A vertical line labeled 'Cut-off' is positioned at a Poverty rate around 59.
- To the left of the cut-off (labeled 'Untreated'), a solid black line shows a slight increase in mortality rate from about 2.2 at poverty rate 20 to about 2.8 at the cut-off, with a surrounding gray 95% confidence interval band that widens near the cut-off (reaching up to approximately 4).
- To the right of the cut-off (labeled 'Treated'), the solid line drops abruptly to around 1.3, peaks slightly around poverty rate 70 at 1.8, and ends near 1.5 at poverty rate 82. The confidence interval band is also shown.

Graph (b), titled '(b) Histogram of poverty rate':
- X-axis: Poverty rate, ranging from 20 to 80.
- Y-axis: Histogram count, ranging from 0 to 160.
- Shows a distribution of observation counts across poverty rates, peaking around 170 at poverty rate 20 and declining steadily down to near 0 above a poverty rate of 70.
- A vertical black line marks the 'Cut-off' at approximately 59, demonstrating no sharp discontinuity or manipulation in the density of observations right around the threshold.

pg_771__page_37_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts illustrating Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity (FRD) design as a function of a 'Running variable' on the horizontal axis from 0.0 to 2.5, with a cutoff point marked at c = 1.0.

Chart (a), titled '(a) Conditional treatment probability', plots 'Probability of treatment' on the vertical axis (0.0 to 1.0) against the running variable. The curve p(x) rises continuously from ~0.07 at x = 0 to 0.3 at the cutoff c = 1.0, where it jumps vertically to 0.7, and then continues rising smoothly toward 1.0 as x increases to 2.5.

Chart (b), titled '(b) Fuzzy regression discontinuity', plots 'Dependent variable' on the vertical axis (0.0 to 1.0). It shows three curves:
1. m0(x): A dashed curve representing the outcome without treatment, rising from 0.4 at x = 0 towards ~0.95 at x = 2.5.
2. m1(x): A dashed straight line representing the outcome under treatment, starting from 0.0 at x = 0 and increasing linearly to ~0.87 at x = 2.5.
3. m(x): A solid curve representing the observed conditional outcome. For X < c (x < 1.0), m(x) lies close to m0(x), reaching about 0.71 at c = 1.0. At the cutoff c = 1.0, m(x) drops abruptly down to approximately 0.56, then rises for X > c (x > 1.0) towards m1(x), nearly coinciding with it as x reaches 2.5.

pg_771__page_45_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 22.1 illustrates the concepts of non-uniform vs. uniform convergence with two side-by-side plots:

(a) Non-uniform convergence: Shows a solid curve representing the true function S(\theta) with a minimum at \theta_0. A sequence of dashed curves S_{n_1}(\theta), S_{n_2}(\theta), and S_{n_3}(\theta) deviate significantly near the right boundary, with local minima at estimates \hat{\theta}_{n_1}, \hat{\theta}_{n_2}, and \hat{\theta}_{n_3} that shift towards the right edge rather than converging to \theta_0.

(b) Uniform convergence: Displays a bold solid curve S(\theta) bounded within an epsilon tube defined by upper and lower dashed envelope curves S(\theta) + \varepsilon and S(\theta) - \varepsilon. An oscillating curve S_n(\theta) stays completely inside this \varepsilon-band around S(\theta), demonstrating that the maximum difference between S_n(\theta) and S(\theta) is controlled uniformly across the domain.

pg_771__page_51_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line graph titled "FIGURE 22.2 Consistency of M-estimator" showing two U-shaped curves representing loss functions as functions of parameter theta. The left curve (solid line) represents the population criterion function S(theta), reaching its global minimum at the point labeled S(theta_0). The right curve (dashed line) represents the sample criterion function S_n(theta), reaching its global minimum at the point labeled S_n(hat_theta). Vertical dotted lines connect corresponding points on the two curves at theta_0 (from S(theta_0) up to S_n(theta_0)) and at hat_theta (from S_n(hat_theta) up to S(hat_theta)). A thick segment on the dashed curve highlights the region between theta_0 and hat_theta.

pg_771__page_55_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line plots side-by-side labeled '(a) Box-cox transformation' and '(b) Regression kink model'.

Plot (a) shows Box-cox transformation curves on a grid where the x-axis is 'Variable' ranging from 0.0 to 2.0 and the y-axis is 'Box-cox transformation' ranging from -1.0 to 1.0. Five lines correspond to different values of lambda:
- lambda = 2 (dash-dot-dot line): starts low and curves upward steeply past 1.0 at x = 2.0.
- lambda = 1 (solid straight line): diagonal line from (0.0, -1.0) to (2.0, 1.0).
- lambda = 0.5 (dashed line): moderately curved line above lambda = 1 for x < 1, and below lambda = 1 for x > 1.
- lambda = 0 (dash-dot line): logarithm-like curve.
- lambda = -1 (long-dashed curve): flattens out horizontally around y = -0.5 for small x values.

Plot (b) illustrates a regression kink model with 'Debt/GDP' on the x-axis (0 to 120) and 'GDP growth rate' on the y-axis (-6 to 6). A solid line increases linearly from around y = 3.4 at x = 0 to a peak near y = 4.9 at x = 44 (marked with a square symbol), after which it kinks and decreases linearly down to below 0 at x = 120. A shaded confidence region surrounds the line, widening significantly as Debt/GDP increases beyond 80.

pg_771__page_57_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 23.2 displays two plots illustrating the average squared error functions used in estimation.

Graph (a), titled '(a) Box-cox regression', plots the Box-cox coefficient (lambda) on the horizontal axis from -2.0 to 1.0 against the Average squared error function S_n(lambda) on the vertical axis from 1.2 to 2.0. The curve decreases to a distinct global minimum around lambda = -0.75, labeled with a point and 'hat lambda', before rising smoothly as lambda increases up to 1.0.

Graph (b), titled '(b) CES production function', is a 2D contour plot showing levels of the average squared error function. The horizontal axis represents parameter rho ranging from -3 to 1, and the vertical axis represents parameter alpha ranging from 0.0 to 0.6. Concentric contour lines curve around a minimum point located near alpha = 0.4 and rho = 0.4, marked by a black dot labeled 'hat theta'.

pg_771__page_64_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 23.3 titled 'Threshold regression: Card-Mas-Rothstein (2008) model' consisting of two side-by-side plots labeled (a) and (b).

Plot (a) Estimation criterion:
- X-axis: 'Threshold coefficient' ranging from 0.1 to 0.5.
- Y-axis: 'Average squared error function' ranging from 3766 to 3772.
- Curve: Shows a line plot representing S_n(gamma) with multiple local minima and maxima, reaching a sharp global minimum around a threshold coefficient value of approximately 0.20 (marked with a point and labeled gamma-hat).

Plot (b) Threshold regression estimates:
- X-axis: 'Fraction minority in 1970' ranging from 0.1 to 0.5.
- Y-axis: 'Change in white population, 1970-1980' ranging from -20 to 20.
- Visualization: Displays a discontinuous regression curve with a confidence region (shaded area) split by a vertical solid line at the estimated threshold of fraction minority = 0.20. To the left of 0.20, the estimated change in white population starts around 14 and slowly decreases to around 10. At 0.20, there is a sharp downward jump to around -2, after which the curve further declines to around -11 before slightly flattening around 0.5.

pg_771__page_67_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line plot titled 'FIGURE 23.4 Test for threshold regression in the Card-Mass-Rothstein model' showing the Threshold F statistic as a function of the Threshold coefficient (ranging from 0.0 to 0.5). The y-axis ranges from 0 to 80. A solid curve representing F_n(gamma) displays a sharp peak reaching approximately 63 at a threshold coefficient of around 0.20, labeled F_n(hat{gamma}). Horizontal dashed reference lines represent 'Multiplier bootstrap 99% critical value' at 75, a 95% critical value line at approximately 56.5, and a 90% critical value line at approximately 48. Outside the main peak around 0.20, the F-statistic curve remains generally below 35 across other threshold coefficient values.

pg_771__page_73_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two comparative plots side by side illustrating loss functions and the Least Absolute Deviations criterion.

Left Plot (a): Titled '(a) Quadratic and absolute loss functions'. The horizontal axis is labeled 'x'. It shows two curves plotted against x: a smooth solid U-shaped curve labeled 'x^2' representing quadratic loss, and a V-shaped dashed line labeled '|x|' representing absolute loss. The two curves intersect away from the origin.

Right Plot (b): Titled '(b) Least Absolute Deviations criterion with n = 7'. The horizontal axis is labeled '\beta' with numerical tick marks at 0.17, 0.18, 0.19, 0.20, 0.21, and 0.22. A piecewise linear curve labeled 'M_n(\beta)' connects 7 data points (marked as small circles). The curve slopes downwards steeply from left to right, reaching a minimum near \beta = 0.196 (indicated by a downward arrow pointing to the x-axis), and then slopes upwards sharply to the right.

pg_771__page_75_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side line plots showing quantile regressions of wage against years of education (ranging from 4 to 20 years). Both plots display five percentile curves: 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%.

Left plot (a) Wage quantile regression: The vertical axis measures 'Dollars per hour' from 0 to 100. Across all education levels, higher percentiles yield higher hourly wages. For 4 to 12 years of education, the curves rise gradually and remain relatively close together (around $5 to $30). As education increases from 12 to 20 years, the wages diverge dramatically, especially for the 90th percentile, which sharply increases to over $100 per hour at 20 years, whereas the 10th percentile rises much more modestly to under $20 per hour.

Right plot (b) Log wage quantile regression: The vertical axis measures 'Log dollars per hour' from 2 to 4. The log transformation linearizes the relationship, showing roughly parallel upward trends across all percentiles as education increases beyond 10 years.

pg_771__page_77_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A plot illustrating the quantile loss function rho_tau(x) for two values of tau: tau = 0.5 and tau = 0.2, plotted against x. The horizontal axis represents x, with the origin where the loss reaches zero. For tau = 0.5 (represented by solid lines), the loss function is symmetric around x = 0, forming a V-shape with equal absolute slopes on both the positive and negative sides. For tau = 0.2 (represented by dashed lines), the loss function is asymmetric: it has a steeper slope for negative values of x (x < 0) and a flatter slope for positive values of x (x > 0).

pg_771__page_78_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 24.4 illustrates two types of quantile curve shapes labeled (a) Linear and (b) Parallel, plotted on axes with Y on the vertical axis and X on the horizontal axis.

In graph (a) Linear, five linear quantile curves radiate outward from a lower point on the Y-axis across increasing X values. The curves represent different quantiles, labeled from bottom to top as q_0.1(x), q_0.3(x), q_0.5(x), q_0.7(x), and q_0.9(x). As X increases, the vertical spread between the quantile lines widens, showing heteroscedasticity.

In graph (b) Parallel, five non-linear (wave-shaped) quantile curves run parallel to each other across X. The curves have identical wavy shapes featuring a local peak followed by a local trough. They are labeled from top to bottom as q_0.9(x), q_0.7(x), q_0.5(x), q_0.3(x), and q_0.1(x), maintaining a constant vertical distance from one another across all values of X.

pg_771__page_83_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side plots comparing quantile regressions for wage against education in (a) Linear model and (b) Logarithmic model, demonstrating quantile crossings.

- Plot (a) Linear model: Plots 'Wage' (y-axis from 0 to 60) against 'Education (years)' (x-axis from 0 to 20). Five straight quantile regression lines corresponding to $q_{0.1}, q_{0.3}, q_{0.5}, q_{0.7},$ and $q_{0.9}$ fan out from right to left. Because they have different slopes and intercepts, the lines cross each other near lower education levels (around 0 to 4 years), illustrating negative fitted values and line crossing in a linear quantile specification.
- Plot (b) Logarithmic model: Plots 'Wage' on the y-axis against 'Education (years)' on the x-axis for the same set of quantiles ($q_{0.1}$ through $q_{0.9}$). The fitted curves display exponential/log-linear growth curves that remain strictly positive and do not cross across the range of education values.

pg_771__page_87_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A line plot titled 'FIGURE 24.6 Log wage quantile regressions' showing the relationship between experience in years on the x-axis (ranging from 0 to 40+) and log dollars per hour on the y-axis (ranging from 2.0 to 4.0).

Five smooth curve lines are plotted representing different quantiles:
- q0.9 (90th percentile): Starts around 2.95 at 0 years, rises smoothly to a peak near 3.8 at 25 years, and slowly decreases to around 3.6 past 40 years.
- q0.7 (70th percentile): Starts around 2.8 at 0 years, peaks around 3.4 at 25 years, and decreases slightly past 40 years.
- q0.5 (50th percentile/median): Starts around 2.6 at 0 years, peaks around 3.2 at 25 years, and slightly decreases past 40 years.
- q0.3 (30th percentile): Starts around 2.4 at 0 years, peaks around 2.9 near 25–30 years, and gently slopes downward.
- q0.1 (10th percentile): Starts around 2.0 at 0 years, peaks early around 2.5 near 10–15 years, and remains relatively flat around 2.4–2.5 across higher years of experience.

pg_771__page_94_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side scatter plots with fitted curves showing the relationship between Age (x-axis, ranging from 20 to 80) and Probability of marriage (y-axis, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0) for college-educated men.

Panel (a) titled '(a) Response probabilities' shows individual data points plotted as dots forming an S-shaped trend that rises sharply from near 0.0 probability around age 20 to approximately 0.8 by age 35, plateaus between ages 35 and 65 around 0.8 to 0.85, and then slightly increases toward 1.0 above age 70, fitted with a single smooth curve.

Panel (b) titled '(b) Binary choice models' overlays four different fitted model curves on the same data points:
- Linear model: shown as a dot-dashed line that increases constantly across the age range, crossing below 0 probability near age 20 and exceeding 1.0 near age 75.
- Probit model: shown as a dashed curve.
- Linear series model: shown as a long-dashed curve.
- Probit series model: shown as a solid line, which closely tracks the non-linear S-curve and plateau pattern of the observed data points.

pg_771__page_112_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two line charts side-by-side comparing marital status probability estimates by age (ranging from 20 to 80) for college-educated women, titled (a) Binary response estimates and (b) Multinomial logit.

In chart (a) Binary response estimates:
- The y-axis represents Probability (0.0 to 1.0) and the x-axis represents Age (20 to 80).
- The 'Total' curve fluctuates slightly around 1.0.
- 'Married' starts near 0.1 at age 20, rises sharply to around 0.74 at age 40, then gently declines to around 0.68 by age 80.
- 'Never married' starts around 0.9 at age 20, drops steeply to about 0.13 around age 40, and levels off under 0.1.
- 'Divorced' starts near 0 at age 20 and steadily increases to nearly 0.3 by age 80.
- 'Separated' remains very low, peaking slightly near age 45 around 0.02 and staying close to 0.

In chart (b) Multinomial logit:
- The axes are identical to chart (a).
- The 'Total' line is perfectly flat at exactly 1.0 across all ages, ensuring probabilities sum to 1.
- The individual category curves ('Married', 'Never married', 'Divorced', 'Separated') closely match the shapes in (a), but smooth out the slight artificial fluctuations in the total sum seen in the binary estimates model.

pg_771__page_120_Diagram_2.jpeg.description: A tree diagram representing a nested choice structure titled 'FIGURE 26.2 Nested choice'. At the top root node is 'Car'. This splits into two branch categories: 'Compact' on the left and 'Sports Utility' on the right. Under 'Compact', the branches lead to two leaf choices: 'Honda Civic' and 'Ford Fusion'. Under 'Sports Utility', the branches lead to two leaf choices: 'Honda CR-V' and 'Ford Escape'.

pg_771__page_127_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 26.3 illustrates an ordered choice model using a cumulative distribution function curve labeled G(ε) plotted against a latent variable U* on the horizontal axis.

The vertical axis represents probabilities corresponding to discrete outcomes Y from 1 to 5, indicated by curly brackets on the left edge:
- P[Y=1] corresponds to the interval from the bottom up to the vertical line at threshold α₁.
- P[Y=2] corresponds to the interval between α₁ and α₂.
- P[Y=3] corresponds to the interval between α₂ and α₃.
- P[Y=4] corresponds to the interval between α₃ and α₄.
- P[Y=5] corresponds to values above α₄.

Horizontal dashed/solid grid lines project from the curve at each threshold point (α₁, α₂, α₃, α₄) back to the vertical axis, dividing the cumulative probability space into five distinct segments corresponding to each value of Y.

pg_771__page_137_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 27.1 illustrates censored densities through two subplots labeled (a) and (b).

Graph (a), titled 'Transfers from abroad', shows a distribution plot of 'Transfers (pesos)' on the horizontal axis ranging from 0 to 20,000. At 0, there is a tall vertical bar indicating a spike at 80%. For values greater than 0, a continuous density curve f(y) represents the remaining 20% of the distribution, which peaks around 2,000-3,000 pesos and tapers off as transfer amounts increase up to 20,000.

Graph (b), titled 'Censoring process', illustrates the theoretical Tobit/censoring model. The horizontal axis represents the latent variable Y*, with a mean at X'β. A normal-shaped density curve f(y) is shown for Y*. A vertical threshold at 0 separates the latent distribution into two parts: the region where Y* ≤ 0 is censored (indicated by a dashed tail accumulating into a single point mass bar at 0 labeled P[Y* = 0]), while the region where Y* > 0 remains an uncensored continuous distribution.

pg_771__page_138_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Figure 27.2 contains two side-by-side plots labeled (a) and (b), illustrating properties of censored distributions.

Graph (a) is titled '(a) Censored regression functions' with the x-axis labeled 'Regressor' (ranging from -3 to 3) and the y-axis labeled 'Dependent variable' (ranging from -4 to 4). It shows a scatter plot of data points categorized into three types:
- Square markers: Y > 0 (uncensored data)
- Open circle markers: Y < 0 (unobserved data below zero)
- Solid circle markers: Y = 0 (censored data along the line y = 0)
It overlays three regression functions:
- Solid line m*(x): the true linear underlying relationship extending below zero.
- Short dashed line m(x): the conditional expectation of the observed censored dependent variable.
- Long dashed line m#(x): another estimated regression curve showing positive values as x decreases.

Graph (b) is titled '(b) Censoring probability' with the x-axis labeled 'Regressor' (ranging from -3 to 3) and the y-axis labeled 'Probability' (ranging from 0.0 to 1.0). It depicts a smooth, decreasing S-shaped curve representing P[Y=0|X], showing that as the regressor x increases, the probability of being censored (Y=0) approaches 0, whereas for negative values of the regressor, the censoring probability approaches 1.0.

pg_771__page_143_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
The image consists of two side-by-side plots labeled (a) and (b), titled together as FIGURE 27.3 Censored regression quantiles.

Plot (a) shows curves corresponding to different quantiles of a dependent variable plotted against an independent variable X, under the specification $Y^* \mid X \sim N(\sqrt{X} - \frac{3}{2}, 2 + X)$. Curves labeled $q_{0.9}(x)$, $q_{0.7}(x)$, $q_{0.5}(x)$, and $q_{0.3}(x)$ fan out upward as X increases. Solid lines represent values above the censoring threshold (a horizontal dashed line), while dashed lines represent values below or subject to censoring.

Plot (b) illustrates the "Effect of income on transfers," displaying four estimation methods plotted against Total income in pesos (ranging from 0 to 200,000) on the x-axis and Transfers in pesos (0 to 12,000) on the y-axis:
- OLS (open squares): Starts high near 12,000+, drops around 20,000, then rises gently to near 8,000 at 200,000 income.
- Tobit (filled squares): Starts near 12,000+, sharply drops to around 3,500 at 50,000 income, and flattens out around 3,500-4,000.
- LAD (filled triangles): Follows a similar steep downward path, flattening out lower than Tobit around 2,000-3,000.
- CLAD (filled circles): Follows the lowest path among the non-OLS curves, dropping steadily to around 1,500 at 200,000 income.

pg_921__page_24_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
Two plots comparing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of various model selection estimators (BIC with n=1000, BIC with n=200, 5% significance test, AIC, and No selection) plotted against the square root of lambda.

Plot (a) MSE, K = 1:
- Y-axis: Mean squared error, ranging from 0 to 4.
- X-axis: square root of lambda, ranging from 0 to 5.
- The 'No selection' line is constant at MSE = 1.
